Triage: lands in `packages/metadata-core` (dispatch predicate) + `packages/drivers/driver-sql` + one caller in `service-messaging` ⇒ `domain:engine`, type `Bug`, **queued** (`pm:queue`).

Not routed to the decision inbox, per the standing meta-criterion: **a silently-dropped caller declaration defaults into the existing loud-refusal family** — this repo has already ruled that shape twice on this exact dispatch predicate (#5748's operator-object `data.id`, #6435), and `ENGINE_UPDATE_OPTION_KEYS` exists precisely to make ignored options loud. The inherited reason transfers cleanly: a predicate the engine will not honour must be refused at authoring time, not evaluated to nothing. So the default route is the card's own option 2 (+3):

1. **Refuse at the engine**: a `by-id` dispatch carrying predicate keys beyond `id` becomes a loud error (same style as the #5748 refusal), in `update` and the `delete` twin.
2. **Move `redeliver` off the trap**: its compare-and-set requirement is real and must survive — re-express the terminal-status guard on a dispatch path that honours the full predicate (mechanism assumption to verify, not a ruling: the predicate/multi path reaches the driver with the whole `where`). Acceptance evidence: a concurrent-claim test — row flips to `in_flight` between read and write ⇒ the reset does NOT land and redeliver reports refusal, not success.
3. **Blast radius measured first**: grep every by-id `update`/`delete` caller passing extra `where` keys. If any caller's guard cannot be expressed on the predicate path, **stop and report the fork** — do not widen the by-id path to honour predicates (that is a capability addition needing its own ruling) and do not quietly leave that caller broken.

Sizing note for the engine seat: M (shared write path + caller migration + refusal pins). Hot-surface note: `sql-driver.ts` also carries queued #10997 and blocked #10998 — fold-or-serial is the seat's five-gate call at claim time.

Lane in-flight at claim: 1.

## ⛔ Clause ② — declared `yes`, and the tier follows from it

This card's adjudicated route is *"a by-id dispatch carrying predicate keys beyond `id` becomes a loud error"*. **That changes contract accept/reject behaviour**: calls that succeed today will throw. It narrows rather than widens, and it is a `declared = enforced` restoration — which is why the *adjudication* correctly stayed out of the decision inbox — but the **tier** mandate is written on content, not on who adjudicated: `dispatch-gates --tier` says it in as many words, *"Clause ② is NOT reachable from paths … judged from the card CONTENT. This line is a FLOOR, never a clearance."*

Dispatched at `CONTRACT_REVIEW_TIER`, read from its single source (`scripts/pm/dispatch-gates.mjs:2722`) rather than recalled, so the enqueue gate is satisfied at dispatch time rather than by attaching `needs:contract-review` afterwards.

## ⛔ Surface correction to triage's landing list — verified, not assumed

Triage routed this to `metadata-core` + `driver-sql` + `service-messaging` and cited `ENGINE_UPDATE_OPTION_KEYS` as the loud-refusal precedent. **That constant is not in `metadata-core`.** Measured on `origin/main` @ `95437e7d2`:

| symbol | actual location |
|:--|:--|
| `ENGINE_UPDATE_OPTION_KEYS` | **`packages/objectql/src/engine.ts:382`**, consumed by `rejectUnknownEngineOptions` at `:9256` |
| `resolveEngineUpdateDispatch` / `assertEngineUpdateDispatch` | `packages/metadata-core/src/engine-update-dispatch.ts` (`:225`) |

So the refusal machinery is **split across two packages**, and a fix written in the style of the cited precedent reaches `objectql` — which triage's list did not name. Recorded because it changes both the file surface and what this card can be dispatched alongside.

(I checked this only because a grep for `ENGINE_UPDATE_OPTION_KEYS` in `metadata-core` returned zero, and a zero-hit is not a reading until a known-present neighbour confirms the query is live. `resolveEngineUpdateDispatch` was the control.)

## Premise re-verified on merged `origin/main` @ `95437e7d2`
`SqlDriver.update(object, id, data, options)` at `:5815`. The card's central claim — that it builds `.where('id', id)` + tenant scope and never applies `options.where` — is the dev's to re-derive at that line.

## Carried into the dispatch order
Triage's route (option 2 + 3) with its **blast-radius-first** clause and its stop-condition: if any by-id caller's guard cannot be expressed on the predicate path, ⛔ do not widen the by-id path to honour predicates (a capability addition needing its own ruling) and ⛔ do not quietly leave that caller broken — stop and report the fork.

## ACCEPT — PR #11147, 31/31 checks green, enqueued

Verified independently rather than read off the report: `mergeable_state: clean`, every check run read **by name** (31 total; `Console Pin Gate` and `Build Docs` **skipped**, not red — this diff touches neither path), `Lint & Repo Gates` green including `check:engine-double-contract`. Flipped to ready, auto-merge enabled.

The triage order's three clauses were all discharged: blast-radius measured **first**, `redeliver` moved off the trap, and the stop-condition — *"if any caller's guard cannot be expressed on the predicate path, stop and report the fork"* — was never reached, because every censused caller's guard **is** expressible there. The by-id driver path was **not** widened. That was the one outcome this dispatch most needed to avoid, and it was avoided for the right reason rather than by luck.

### ⚠️ One deviation from the literal dispatch order, accepted — recording it so it is not found later as undocumented drift

Triage's route said a by-id dispatch carrying predicate keys beyond `id` **becomes a loud error**. The implementation makes that true for three of four cells, but routes the fourth — `where: { id, …extra }` **with a declared `multi: true`** — silently to the predicate path instead of refusing it. That is a behaviour change shipped *without* a diagnostic: a caller who wrote that shape previously got an unconditional single-row write and now gets a conditional multi-row one.

Accepted, for three reasons in descending weight:

1. **It is not a widening.** `multi: true` is the caller explicitly declaring predicate semantics; compiling their whole `where` is what they asked for. Refusing it would refuse a correctly-spelled compare-and-set.
2. **The cell ships with no occupants** — the census reports zero callers anywhere, and I spot-checked that independently (every `multi: true` hit sharing a line with `id` across non-test `packages/**` is a comment, a dispatch case-table row, or an `$in` id set; none is a scalar-id-plus-extra-keys call). ⚠️ My check is line-based and strictly cruder than the dev's balanced-paren scanner — it found nothing contradicting the census, which is weaker than confirming it.
3. The changeset states the change per call shape, so release-notes readers meet it.

⛔ Had the census found even one occupant, this cell would have gone back for a refusal or a ruling. It is the emptiness that makes silence acceptable here, not the reasoning alone.

### ⛔ My scoping error, not the dev's

I declared the file surface as four packages including **`packages/drivers/driver-sql/src/sql-driver.ts`**. The landed PR touches 16 files and **`sql-driver.ts` is not among them** — the fix lives in the shared dispatch predicates, exactly where it should, and the driver never needed changing.

Consequence: I serialized **#11101** and **#11067** against a file that was never at risk for the whole life of this dispatch. Over-declaring a surface is not the safe direction of error I had been treating it as — it costs throughput just as under-declaring costs safety, and it does so invisibly. **Correction to this seat's practice: a declared surface is a prediction, and when a dev's actual surface lands narrower, the seat releases the serial hold instead of leaving it standing to the merge.**

### Residual, correctly escalated rather than decided

**#11142** — a scalar `data.id` beside a *different* scalar `where.id` still silently drops the `where.id`. The dev declined to fix it because doing so reverses a **pinned #5748 verdict** (the `expectId` case), and that distinction is right: refusing `data.id` + non-id keys does not touch #5748's precedence rule, while refusing `data.id` + `where.id` would overturn it. Labelled `finding` and left for triage — ⛔ note for the grading round that this is a **decision-inbox shape, not an ordinary observation**: it is the last surviving cell of the exact silent-predicate-loss class this PR just closed, so grading it as "no user impact today" would be the wrong read.

Excellent work — particularly measuring both defect behaviours as passing assertions on the unfixed tree *before* any edit.
